concept.name: Last trading day
concept.definition: The final day on which a futures or options contract may be traded on the exchange; after the close of the last trading day, remaining open positions proceed to settlement or delivery.
concept.intuition: The last trading day is the deadline for closing a position on your own terms — miss it, and the contract's settlement machinery decides the outcome for you.
concept.mechanics: Each product's specification fixes the last trading day: for standard U.S. equity options it is the expiration Friday (third Friday of the month), while for many European-style index options it is the Thursday before expiration Friday; futures contracts typically stop trading a set number of days before or within the delivery month, after which delivery or final cash settlement occurs.
concept.failure_modes: Positions held past the last trading day lose the ability to be closed competitively and are exposed to the exchange's settlement procedure, which can produce prices far from recent trades; low liquidity on the last day also degrades exit quality.
concept.misconceptions: The last trading day is not always the same as the expiration date — for many index options trading stops the day before expiration — and it differs by product, so assuming the equity-option convention generalizes is unsafe.
concept.example: A trader long a European-style index call who wants out must sell by the Thursday before expiration Friday; after that close, only the expiration-day settlement value determines the payoff.
